claim: Because its parameters carry model size and data size explicitly, the derived law picks better data mixtures than empirical laws and can choose a mixture for a larger, unseen scale from small-scale runs alone. Supported only if, at fixed scale, the mixture it predicts gives the lowest held-out perplexity among the mixtures predicted by four empirical laws and the uniform mixture in every setting tested (4 domains at 200M parameters; 7 SlimPajama domains at 122M and 310M; Pile-CC loss in the 17-domain setting); and if, fitted only on small-scale runs, the mixture it extrapolates to the larger scale (700M on 16B tokens; 1B on 30B tokens) beats the mixture it would choose at the small scale and is at least as good as the additive law's mixture, even when that law was fitted with runs at the target scale.

experiments: Derive the model. Setup: extend the quantization model of scaling laws to K domains whose skills have power-law frequencies with a shared head and disjoint tails: a model of capacity N allocates units across domains, giving a closed-form allocation x_i*(h) under similar exponents and domain loss c_i x_i*^(-b_i) that depends on all weights through an aggregate-demand term. Extend projected linear regression trained by one-pass SGD to the same structure: L_i(h | N, D) ~ c_i x_i*(h, N)^(-b_i) + A_i (D h_i)^(-a_i) + E_i (Theorem 4.1). Find the optimal mixture for target weights w by bi-level optimisation with online mirror descent using a closed-form gradient (Proposition 4.2).

Choose the optimal mixture at fixed scale. Setup: target = uniform over domains; settings: 4 domains (Wikipedia, GitHub, StackExchange, PG-19) with 25 mixtures on 200M LLaMA-style models for 8B tokens, cosine schedule; 7-domain SlimPajama at 122M / 10B and 310M / 20B with constant learning rate (data from prior work); 17-domain Pile with Pile-CC as the target; fit every applicable law, solve for h* (cvxpy or L-BFGS), and train new models on each predicted mixture. Result: the derived law's mixture gives the lowest test perplexity in all three perplexity settings and lower Pile-CC loss than the additive law's mixture (figures; no numbers reported).

Extrapolate to larger scales. Setup: fit only on small-scale runs (200M / 8B for 4 domains; 122M / 10B for 7 domains), then plug in the target scale (700M / 16B; 1B / 30B) to compute an extrapolated mixture; compare with the mixture optimal for the small scale and with the additive law's mixture (fitted at 200M / 8B for 4 domains, where its optimum is scale-invariant; for 7 domains, the published mixture fitted on 412M-1.4B models and 4B-46B tokens, including the 1B / 30B target). Result: at 700M / 16B the extrapolated mixture has the lowest test loss, below both alternatives; at 1B / 30B it beats the small-scale mixture and matches the additive law's full-data mixture (training-loss curves).

Note limits of the evidence. Setup: fitting accuracy is measured on one reused 64-model Pile dataset; four of 17 domains use training loss as the held-out proxy; the 7-domain results reuse another paper's runs; mixture comparisons are reported only as single-run perplexity bars and loss curves without seeds; the fitting problem is non-convex and sensitive to initialisation (multiple random restarts). The theory assumes one-pass SGD on linear regression while experiments train transformers with AdamW and cosine or constant schedules.
